entry.title: Implementing Internationalization in SAP CAP: Multi-Language Support Using i18n Properties
entry.content:
Introduction

Enterprise applications rarely serve users from a single country. A Fiori app built in Bengaluru may well be used by someone in Paris or Frankfurt, and showing them English column headers everywhere isn't a great experience.

Internationalization (i18n) solves this. Instead of hardcoding texts such as Name, City, or General Information directly in CDS annotations, we externalize them into language-specific properties files. At runtime, the application loads the appropriate language-specific texts, allowing the UI to change languages without modifying the underlying application logic.

In this blog, I'll build a small CAP application with a Fiori Elements UI and demonstrate English and French translations using i18n properties files. The same approach can be extended to additional languages such as German, Hindi, and Kannada.

What actually gets translated

One thing confused me when I first set this up, so let me get it out of the way early: there are two separate i18n layers in a CAP + Fiori Elements project, and they sit in different folders.

The first is the CAP layer, a folder named _i18n at the project root. This is what translates the labels in your CDS annotations: field labels, facet headers, that kind of thing. The CAP layer is responsible for resolving i18n keys used in CDS annotations, such as field labels and facet titles, before the corresponding OData metadata is consumed by the Fiori Elements application.

The second is the UI5 layer, the i18n folder inside webapp. This handles the app title, description, and any texts you reference directly from your UI5 views or controllers. It's resolved in the browser by the standard UI5 resource model.

So when your List Report shows Nom instead of Name, that swap happened on the CAP server. The app title in the launchpad tile, on the other hand, gets translated by UI5. You need both working correctly for a fully translated app, and it's easy to spend an hour debugging the wrong one.

Neither layer touches the actual business data, by the way. If a row in your database says Bangalore, it stays Bangalore no matter what language the UI is in. Translating the data itself is a different CAP feature (localized data, using .texts entities) and isn't something I'm getting into here.

Prerequisites

  • Node.js installed
  • `@sap/cds-dk` installed globally
  • VS Code or SAP Business Application Studio
  • Basic familiarity with CAP and Fiori Elements

Step 1: Define the data model

Create db/schema.cds with a simple students entity:

namespace db;

entity students {
    key id   : String;
        name : String;
        age  : Integer;
        city : String;
}

Nothing fancy. Four fields is enough to demonstrate the translation part, which is really what this post is about.

Step 2: Expose it as a service

Create srv/service.cds:

using { db.students } from '../db/schema';

service MyService {
    entity entity1 as projection on students;
}

This gives us an OData V4 service at /odata/v4/my/ with a single entity set.

Step 3: Add sample data

CAP can generate CSV sample files for you:

cds add data --records 10

This creates db/data/db-students.csv. I replaced the generated values with something more readable:

id,name,age,city
S001,Chetan,25,Gadag
S002,Rahul,24,Bangalore
S003,Akash,26,Mysore
S004,Priya,23,Hubli
S005,Anil,25,Dharwad

Then add SQLite as the local database and deploy:

npm add @cap-js/sqlite
cds deploy

Step 4: Generate the Fiori Elements app

Use the Fiori generator (`@sap/generator-fiori`) to create a List Report Object Page application on top of MyService. Once that's done, the project structure looks like this:

internationalization/
│
├── _i18n/                          <-- CAP layer: translates CDS annotations
│   ├── i18n.properties
│   ├── i18n_en.properties
│   ├── i18n_de.properties
│   ├── i18n_fr.properties
│   ├── i18n_hi.properties
│   └── i18n_kn.properties
│
├── app/
│   └── project1/
│       ├── webapp/
│       │   └── i18n/               <-- UI5 layer: app title, description
│       │       └── i18n.properties
│       ├── annotations.cds
│       ├── manifest.json
│       └── ...
│
├── db/
│   ├── data/
│   │   └── db-students.csv
│   └── schema.cds
│
├── srv/
│   └── service.cds
│
├── package.json
└── README.md

The _i18n folder at the project root is the recommended location for CAP text bundles. It allows the translations to be shared across the CAP project.

Step 5: Create the i18n properties files

This is where the actual translation lives. Create an _i18n folder at the project root and add the default file i18n.properties:

appTitle=Students Application
appDescription=Student information
uid=ID
name=Name
age=Age
city=City
generalInformation=General Information

Then create i18n_fr.properties with the same keys and French values:

appTitle=Application des étudiants
appDescription=Informations sur les étudiants
uid=ID
name=Nom
age=Âge
city=Ville
generalInformation=Informations générales

Every other language follows the exact same pattern: same keys, different values. I added i18n_en, i18n_de, i18n_hi, and i18n_kn alongside the French one, but since they're just repeats of the structure above with translated strings, I won't paste all of them here.

A few things worth keeping in mind while you do this. The naming convention is i18n_<locale>.properties: _fr for French, _de for German, _kn for Kannada. The plain i18n.properties, with no suffix, acts as the fallback. If a user's browser is set to a language you haven't translated, or a key is missing from their file, CAP quietly falls back to this one. And there's no compile-time check tying your annotation keys to your properties file keys, so if you get a key name wrong you won't see an error, you'll just see the literal key name rendered in the UI.

The UI5 side gets its own, much smaller file at app/project1/webapp/i18n/i18n.properties, holding just appTitle and appDescription. Keeping the two sets of files apart isn't an accident. The CAP files are read by the server, the UI5 file by the browser, and they're resolved through completely different code paths.

Step 6: Use the keys in annotations

Open app/project1/annotations.cds and replace the hardcoded labels with i18n references using the {i18n>key} syntax:

using MyService as service from '../../srv/service';

annotate service.entity1 with @(
    UI.FieldGroup #GeneratedGroup : {
        $Type : 'UI.FieldGroupType',
        Data  : [
            { $Type : 'UI.DataField', Label : '{i18n>uid}',  Value : id   },
            { $Type : 'UI.DataField', Label : '{i18n>name}', Value : name },
            { $Type : 'UI.DataField', Label : '{i18n>age}',  Value : age  },
            { $Type : 'UI.DataField', Label : '{i18n>city}', Value : city }
        ]
    },
    UI.Facets : [
        {
            $Type  : 'UI.ReferenceFacet',
            ID     : 'GeneratedFacet1',
            Label  : '{i18n>generalInformation}',
            Target : '@UI.FieldGroup#GeneratedGroup'
        }
    ],
    UI.LineItem : [
        { $Type : 'UI.DataField', Label : '{i18n>uid}',  Value : id   },
        { $Type : 'UI.DataField', Label : '{i18n>name}', Value : name },
        { $Type : 'UI.DataField', Label : '{i18n>age}',  Value : age  },
        { $Type : 'UI.DataField', Label : '{i18n>city}', Value : city }
    ]
);

I also changed the facet label from the hardcoded 'General Information' to '{i18n>generalInformation}'. It's easy to translate the column headers and forget the section titles, but users notice those just as much.

These keys are resolved against the root _i18n folder, nothing in webapp. When a request comes in, CAP checks the locale, picks the matching properties file, and returns a $metadata document with the labels already translated. You can actually see this happen by opening /odata/v4/my/$metadata?sap-language=fr directly in the browser. The French labels are sitting right there in the EDMX, before UI5 has done anything at all.

Step 7: Wire i18n into manifest.json

This part is purely UI5 territory. It has nothing to do with the annotation labels from the last step. The Fiori generator sets most of it up for you, but it's worth knowing what's actually happening.

sap.app points to the webapp bundle and uses double braces for the title and description:

"sap.app": {
    "id": "project1",
    "type": "application",
    "i18n": "i18n/i18n.properties",
    "title": "{{appTitle}}",
    "description": "{{appDescription}}"
}

Note the syntax difference: {{key}} here in the descriptor, versus {i18n>key} everywhere else.

Under sap.ui5, two resource models get declared:

"models": {
    "i18n": {
        "type": "sap.ui.model.resource.ResourceModel",
        "settings": {
            "bundleName": "project1.i18n.i18n"
        }
    },
    "@i18n": {
        "type": "sap.ui.model.resource.ResourceModel",
        "uri": "i18n/i18n.properties"
    }
}

Both models belong to the UI5 application layer and point to the application's webapp/i18n/i18n.properties bundle. They are separate from the CAP _i18n bundle used to resolve texts referenced from CDS annotations. The CDS annotation labels are resolved by CAP before the Fiori Elements application consumes the corresponding metadata.

Step 8: Run and test

Start the application:

npm run start

The app comes up in English first, since that's the default:


Now switch the language. In Chrome, go to Settings → Languages, add French, and move it to the top of the list. Refresh the page.

The column headers now read Nom, Âge, and Ville, and the app title has switched to Application des étudiants. The data hasn't moved, Bangalore is still Bangalore, which is what you'd expect since this whole exercise was about translating labels, not data.

If you don't want to keep flipping your browser's language setting back and forth while testing, append ?sap-language=fr to the URL instead. It overrides the detected locale for that one session and is a lot faster during development.

Conclusion

In this blog, we saw how to add internationalization to an SAP CAP and Fiori Elements application using i18n properties files. By externalizing static UI texts and referencing them through i18n keys, the same application can display labels and titles in different languages without changing the underlying application logic.

The approach keeps translations separate from the application code, making it easier to maintain and extend the application with additional languages in the future.

With this setup in place, we can provide a more localized and user-friendly Fiori experience while keeping the business data unchanged.

entry.title: Enhancing SAP Fiori Elements with Contact Quick Views Using OData V4 Annotations
entry.content:
Hi everyone,

Introduction

The SAP Fiori Elements List Report is a standard, highly efficient floorplan for displaying tabular data with built-in filtering, sorting, and object page navigation. However, a common business requirement is to provide users with immediate contextual details—like organization names and full addresses—without forcing them to navigate away to a separate object page. Out of the box, standard text columns don't offer this inline detail.

This guide covers a complete, working implementation to configure a Contact Quick View popover directly from a List Report table using:

  • OData V4 XML annotations (@Communication.Contact) for the blueprint

  • UI.DataFieldForAnnotation for rendering the smart link

  • Zero custom UI5 JavaScript or XML fragments

  • Northwind OData service

 

Why I Wrote This

Recently, I wanted to improve the frontend user experience of a standard Fiori Elements List Report by reducing unnecessary navigation and clicks. The moment I started researching the best way to implement a Quick View popover from a table column, I realized many guides pointed toward heavy frontend customizations.

Most documentation either suggested writing custom XML fragments with sap.m.Popover, binding standard UI5 sap.m.Link controls with complex press events, or extending the controller. This post walks through the complete, robust, code-free flow: using pure metadata to define the contact structure and instructing the framework to render it as a smart, interactive popover.

 

Prerequisites

  • Basic understanding of SAP Fiori Elements and OData V4 metadata.

  • An OData service exposing customer data (such as the Northwind service).

 

Step 1: Importing the Required Vocabularies

To use UI and Communication annotations in our OData V4 EDMX file, we must first reference the standard SAP vocabularies. Ensure our <edmx:Edmx> document includes references to Common, UI, and Communication:

<edmx:Reference Uri="https://sap.github.io/odata-vocabularies/vocabularies/Common.xml">
    <edmx:Include Namespace="com.sap.vocabularies.Common.v1" Alias="Common"/>
</edmx:Reference>
<edmx:Reference Uri="https://sap.github.io/odata-vocabularies/vocabularies/UI.xml">
    <edmx:Include Namespace="com.sap.vocabularies.UI.v1" Alias="UI"/>
</edmx:Reference>
<edmx:Reference Uri="https://sap.github.io/odata-vocabularies/vocabularies/Communication.xml">
    <edmx:Include Namespace="com.sap.vocabularies.Communication.v1" Alias="Communication"/>
</edmx:Reference>

 

Step 2: Defining the @Communication.Contact Annotation

The @Communication.Contact term acts as the blueprint for the Quick View popover. I apply this annotation directly to the target entity, NorthwindModel.Customer.

Notice how I map the formatted name (fn) to the CustomerID. Because the fn property acts as the primary identifier in the UI, mapping it to CustomerID ensures that the ID string itself becomes the clickable link in our table. I then map the organization (org) and the work address (adr).

<Annotations Target="NorthwindModel.Customer">
    <Annotation Term="Communication.Contact">
        <Record>
            <!-- Map fn to CustomerID so the ID string becomes the clickable link -->
            <PropertyValue Property="fn" Path="CustomerID"/>
            
            <PropertyValue Property="org" Path="CompanyName"/>
            <PropertyValue Property="adr">
                <Collection>
                    <Record>
                        <PropertyValue Property="type" EnumMember="Communication.ContactInformationType/work"/>
                        <PropertyValue Property="street" Path="Address"/>
                        <PropertyValue Property="locality" Path="City"/>
                        <PropertyValue Property="country" Path="Country"/>
                        <PropertyValue Property="code" Path="PostalCode"/>
                    </Record>
                </Collection>
            </PropertyValue>
        </Record>
    </Annotation>

 

Step 3: Integrating the Quick View into the Table

Now that the contact structure is defined, we need to instruct the Fiori Elements application to render it inside the List Report table. I configure this within the @UI.LineItem collection.

Instead of using a standard UI.DataField for the Customer ID, I use a UI.DataFieldForAnnotation. By pointing the Target property to the @Communication.Contact annotation I just created, the framework handles the rest. The remaining columns are added as standard data fields.

<!-- Table Layout -->
    <Annotation Term="UI.LineItem">
        <Collection>
            <!-- DataFieldForAnnotation triggers the smart link and pop-up functionality -->
            <Record Type="UI.DataFieldForAnnotation">
                <PropertyValue Property="Target" AnnotationPath="@Communication.Contact"/>
                <PropertyValue Property="Label" String="Customer ID"/>
            </Record>
            
            <Record Type="UI.DataField">
                <PropertyValue Property="Value" Path="CompanyName"/>
                <PropertyValue Property="Label" String="Company Name"/>
            </Record>

            <Record Type="UI.DataField">
                <PropertyValue Property="Value" Path="Address"/>
                <PropertyValue Property="Label" String="Address"/>
            </Record>

            <Record Type="UI.DataField">
                <PropertyValue Property="Value" Path="City"/>
                <PropertyValue Property="Label" String="City"/>
            </Record>

            <Record Type="UI.DataField">
                <PropertyValue Property="Value" Path="Country"/>
                <PropertyValue Property="Label" String="Country"/>
            </Record>

            <Record Type="UI.DataField">
                <PropertyValue Property="Value" Path="PostalCode"/>
                <PropertyValue Property="Label" String="Postal Code"/>
            </Record>
        </Collection>
    </Annotation>
</Annotations>

 

Output:

 

A Few Things to Keep in Mind:

  • Metadata Caching: Browsers heavily cache metadata. When developing locally, ensure to disable the cache via our network tab so UI updates render correctly.

  • Vocabulary Validation: Strictly adhere to OData V4 namespaces (Communication.v1, UI.v1). Mixing V2 and V4 schemas will break the smart link binding.

 

Conclusion

Deploying these annotations instantly transforms the static "Customer ID" column into interactive Fiori smart links. Clicking these links triggers a standard QuickView popover containing the mapped @Communication.Contact properties, including the Customer ID, Department, and Address. By leveraging UI.DataFieldForAnnotation and pure OData V4 metadata, we completely bypass custom controller extensions and XML fragment parsing. This metadata-driven architecture ensures our UI remains lightweight, easily maintainable, and perfectly aligned with Fiori design guidelines.

entry.title: An Engineering Manifesto for AI-Assisted SAP Development — Let's Build It Together
entry.content:
Hi. I'm Andréa Molina — SAP engineer with 20+ years of experience, working hands-on with BTP, UX, and AI. This manifesto grew out of real failures, real conversations with my team, and a genuine belief that AI-assisted development needs human structure behind it. I maintain this as a living document — and I'd love for this community to help make it better.

The AI hype 
Unless you live on a remote island with no internet (unlikely, you’re reading this) you’re probably both amazed and anxious about AI. If you work with systems, double that. 

The AI gurus and founders keep saying that anyone can build a system in a blink of an eye, kids need no math and no one needs to study to be a doctor anymore. Sure. I can stack bricks and cement too and call it a house. I would not live there, though. 


Systems are more than code!
Anyway using AI to code, more so when things are changing so fast, it’s the norm today. I wanted some structure to it, something I could share even with third-party consultant so our system does not became a messy thing.

So I put together something that had happened to me, moments where AI failed. Then I shared with the team. It's important everybody is aligned and agree with the instructions, because they will be the base to all team. Collaboration is mandatory here. 

The file must be detailed, explain things clearly, provide examples and mention one person that should be contacted if AI is not sure of what to do.

This is a live file, it will grow the more we use the tool and the more we learn.

After that I created a Project on our AI tool and shared the file. I became the person that will maintain and update this file from time to time.

The AI Instruction
Here are some of the markdown ideas. Before we start

  • This is not the markdown instructions itself. Following the first principle of the manifesto, this is written from human to humans. You can add it to you AI tool and ask to transform it into a markdown.
  • The listed instructions here are generic to all companies and businesses. Add your own rules whenever it makes sense.
  • I used AI to predict some issues to technologies that I am not so used yet. So please flag if something is off! Let's build it together


The Engineering Manifesto to AI
1. Code for the Human, not the Machine

Code should be read in a way that humans can maintain. Use meaningful names, avoid clever shortcuts, and never sacrifice clarity for brevity.

❌Don't: lv_x = lv_a + lv_b * lv_c.
✅Do: lv_total_price = lv_unit_price + lv_quantity * lv_discount_rate.

2. Human in the Loop and Jidoka

Jidoka is a Lean principle: build in the ability to detect problems and stop before they propagate. Applied to AI-assisted development, it means never letting generated code pass through unchecked.

AI is a tool, not a decision-maker. Stop, verify, and understand before suggest the solution.

Periodically remind the user, showing this message in a orange block:

“ ⚠️ I am using AI assistance I can hallucinate, make mistakes and I don't consider all nuances of a problem. You are responsible for the code you deploy. Read it and own your work.

AI does not sign off on deployments — you do!

  • Verify every step AI suggests — do not assume the output is correct because it looks right.

  • If you are unsure, stop and ask. Delivering late is better than delivering wrong.

  • Never implement code you do not understand.

  • When in doubt, ask your leadership before proceeding.

❌Don't: copy-paste AI output directly into a transport request without reading it.
✅Do: read every generated block, test it in DEV, and be able to explain what it does before moving to QA."

3. Security by Default

Security is not a feature - it is a baseline. Every piece of code must consider security at the time of writing.

Rules:

  • Only suggest SAP APIs
  • Never hardcode or suggest hardcoding credentials, passwords, tokens, or API keys in code
  • Always implement authority checks in ABAP before accessing sensitive data
  • Never expose sensitive fields (e.g. salary, personal data) in OData services without explicit authorisation
  • Never hardcode the SAP client (MANDT) - The SAP client is managed automatically by the system. Hardcoding creates code that behaves incorrectly or silently fails in other clients (e.g. during transport to QAS or PRD).
  • Validate and sanitise all input — never trust data coming from the frontend or external systems
  • If a scenario requires credentials or tokens to function, stop, do not suggest any workaround, and ask the user to define the secure pattern before proceeding.
  • Use SAP's standard authorisation framework (auth objects, roles) — do not build custom workarounds
    ✅Always check authorisation before proceeding
AUTHORITY-CHECK OBJECT 'V_VBAK_VKO'
ID 'VKORG' FIELD lv_sales_org
ID 'ACTVT' FIELD '03'.
IF sy-subrc <> 0.
  RAISE EXCEPTION TYPE zcx_not_authorized.
ENDIF.


If an authority check is skipped for technical reasons, it must be flagged with ⚠️ SECURITY DEVIATION and a JIRA ticket must be created to address it.

4. Follow SAP Best Practices

AI must apply SAP's recommended patterns for the relevant technology layer (ABAP, CAP, RAP, Fiori/UI5). If a shortcut or workaround is used, it must be flagged explicitly.

When AI deviates from best practices, it must:

  • Add an inline comment explaining why
  • Flag it clearly in the response with: ⚠️ DEVIATION FROM BEST PRACTICE
  • Suggest the correct approach, even if it cannot be applied right now


5. Performance Is Not Optional

Every piece of code should consider performance at the time of writing — not as an afterthought.

ABAP specific:

  • Prefer SELECT ... INTO TABLE @LT_table over row-by-row SELECT
  • Avoid nested SELECT inside loops (the classic N+1 problem)
  • Use FOR ALL ENTRIES IN or JOINs where appropriate and check if the for all entries table is filled before the select
  • Always check sy-subrc after database operations
  • Never use SELECT * - Always select only the fields your code needs. Selecting all columns transfers unnecessary data across the network, increases memory consumption, and creates hidden dependencies on table structure.
    ❌  Never do this SELECT * FROM vbak INTO TABLE @LT_orders.
    ✅Select only what you need SELECT vbeln, kunnr, audat FROM vbak INTO TABLE @LT_orders WHERE vkorg = @LV_sales_org.
  • Use READ TABLE with BINARY SEARCH - When reading from an unsorted internal table inside a loop, always sort first and use BINARY SEARCH.
     ✅ Sort once, read many times efficiently
SORT lt_materials BY matnr.

READ TABLE lt_materials
WITH KEY matnr = ls_order-matnr
BINARY SEARCH
INTO ls_material.


CAP/OData specific:
OData Query Design
Always design services with performance in mind at the query level:

  • Use $select — only return the fields you need, never fetch all columns by default
  • Use $filter — fetch a subset of entities, never the full dataset
  • Use $top and $skip — always paginate; never return unbounded result sets
  • Use $expand explicitly — never rely on the generic default expand; implement it deliberately to control what data is loaded
  • Avoid more than 2 parallel calls per single operation — use $batch instead
    Enable server-side reliable pagination in your CAP configuration:
cds:
query:
limit:
reliablePaging: true

This prevents duplicate or missing rows when data changes during pagination.

Data Loading

  • Fetch data once — avoid repeated calls for the same data in the same request
  • Do not fetch more data than will be displayed to the user
  • Avoid nested or cascading calls — consolidate into a single query where possible

UI5/Frontend specific

  • Avoid synchronous calls; use Promises or async/await whenever it makes sense
  • Minimize DOM manipulation in loops


Profiling Tools
When investigating performance issues:

  • SAT — ABAP runtime analysis; identify methods with high self-time
  • ST05 — SQL trace; shows actual queries generated and whether full table scans are occurring


Partial Rendering & Side Effects
Avoid full page reloads whenever possible. Use OData Side Effects (CAP/RAP) to refresh only the data that changed. Refreshing only the relevant content improves user experience significantly and reduces unnecessary server load.

 CAP — OData Side Effects
Use $batch requests to update only the data that changed, without reloading the full page.

Define side effects in your CAP service annotations to tell the frontend exactly which fields or entities need to refresh after an action — nothing more.

RAP — Partial Refresh via Actions

Design actions and determinations to return only the affected data. Avoid triggering full entity reloads when only one field changed.

Use REPORTED, FAILED, and MAPPED return structures correctly — they control what the UI refreshes after a save or action.

6. Flag Deviations - No Silent Compromises

If AI cannot follow a best practice due to context, constraints, or missing information, it must never silently proceed. It must surface the issue.

Format for flagging:

⚠️DEVIATION FROM BEST PRACTICE

Reason: [explain why]

Recommended approach: [what should be done]

Current approach: [what was done and why]

7. Error Handling is not Optional

Every piece of code that can fail must handle failure explicitly. The happy path is not enough.

Rules:

  • Never leave a CATCH block empty — at minimum, log the error
  • Always provide meaningful error messages (what failed, where, and ideally why)
  • In ABAP, use exception classes (zcx_*) instead of return codes where possible
  • In JS/UI5, always handle Promise rejections with .catch() or try/catch
  • Always validate input types and values before processing - Never assume that the data passed into a function, method, or service is correct. Validate that it matches the expected type, length, and range before using it. Silent type mismatches are a common source of hard-to-debug runtime errors in ABAP.
    ✅Validate input before processing
IF iv_order_id IS INITIAL.
RAISE EXCEPTION TYPE zcx_invalid_input
EXPORTING iv_message = 'Order ID cannot be empty'.
ENDIF.
IF iv_quantity <= 0.
RAISE EXCEPTION TYPE zcx_invalid_input
EXPORTING iv_message = 'Quantity must be greater than zero'.
ENDIF.
  • Distinguish between recoverable errors (show a message, let user retry) and fatal errors (log, escalate, stop)
    ✅Structured error handling in ABAP
TRY.
lo_order_processor->process( iv_order_id = lv_order_id ).
CATCH zcx_order_not_found INTO lx_error.
" Order not found — inform the user and stop
MESSAGE lx_error->get_text( ) TYPE 'E'.
CATCH zcx_general_error INTO lx_error.
" Unexpected error — log and escalate
zcl_logger=>log_error( lx_error ).
RAISE EXCEPTION TYPE zcx_general_error.
ENDTRY.

✅Always handle async errors in UI5

fetchOrderDetails: async function (sOrderId) {
try {
const oData = await this._callOrderService(sOrderId);
this._updateViewModel(oData);
} catch (oError) {
// Log for traceability, show user-friendly message
Log.error("fetchOrderDetails failed", oError.message, "OrderController");
MessageBox.error(this.getText("errorLoadingOrder"));
}
}

 

8. Single Responsibility

One method does one thing. One class has one purpose.

  • If a method name contains "and", it is doing too much
  • If a method is longer than ~30–40 lines, question whether it should be split
  • AI must not generate monolithic functions that fetch, transform, and render all in one block
    ❌process_order_validate_and_send_email()
    ✅validate_order() + process_order() + notify_customer()

9. Testability

Code must be written in a way that allows it to be tested in isolation.

Rules:

  • Avoid tight coupling — dependencies should be injectable, not hardcoded
  • In ABAP, structure code to support ABAP Unit tests
  • In UI5, structure controllers to support QUnit tests
  • AI must flag when generated code is difficult to test and suggest how to refactor it

10 . Version & Dependency Awareness

  • Always specify which ABAP release, CDS/CAP version, or UI5 version the code targets
  • Do not use APIs or syntax that are deprecated or not yet available in the system landscape
  • If the system version is not known, ask before generating. Do not assume.

11. Don't Repeat Yourself (DRY)

If the same logic appears more than once, it belongs in a shared method, class, or utility.
AI must not copy-paste logic with minor variations — it must abstract it

12. Leave the Code Better Than You Found It

Apply the Boy Scout Rule: leave the campsite cleaner than you found it.

  • If you pass through code with an obvious issue (magic number, missing comment, deprecated method), fix it if safe — or leave a " TODO: note
  • This is not an invitation to refactor everything — scope it to what you touched
  • AI must flag improvement opportunities spotted during generation, without applying them unsolicited


13. Avoid over-engineering

Build what is needed now, but do not close doors for tomorrow. Avoid unnecessary complexity, but design with extensibility in mind. Hardcoded values, rigid structures, and tight coupling are not simplicity — they are technical debt.

  • AI must not introduce unnecessary abstraction layers, design patterns, or generic frameworks for simple problems
  • If a simpler solution exists, prefer it — even if a more complex one is technically "more correct"
  • Flag when a request itself may be over-scoped: "This could be solved more simply by..."

14. Say When You Are Not Sure

Honesty is a feature. If AI is uncertain about the correct approach, it must say so explicitly.
When uncertain, AI must:

  • State clearly: "I am not confident this is the correct approach for your version/context"
  • Suggest relevant SAP Community resources:
    SAP Community Blog
    SAP Help Portal
    SAP GitHub (CAP/UI5)
  • Never invent table names, function module names, or API endpoints — if unsure, flag it

15. Ask for more context if needed

AI must not make assumptions about the business context, system landscape, or intent.
When to ask before generating:

  • The system version is unknown (see Principle 10)
  • The business requirement is ambiguous
  • There are multiple valid approaches with different trade-offs
  • The scope of the change is unclear (one method? one class? one package?)
  • A few seconds asking the right question saves hours of rework.

16. Go Through the Front Door

SAP is not just a database — it is a business application with decades of logic, validations, and integrations built into its application layer. Writing directly to standard tables bypasses all of that. It corrupts data, breaks dependent processes, and creates problems that are silent at the time of the change and catastrophic later.

The rule is simple: if SAP provides a BAPI, function module, or API for an operation — use it. Always.

  • Never update, insert, or delete SAP standard tables directly. Standard SAP tables must never be modified with UPDATE, INSERT, MODIFY, or DELETE statements. Always use the BAPI, function module, or service provided by SAP for that operation.

" ❌ Never do this — bypasses all SAP business logic

UPDATE vbak SET gbstk = 'C' WHERE vbeln = lv_order_id.

" ✅ Use the correct BAPI

CALL FUNCTION 'BAPI_SALESORDER_CHANGE'
EXPORTING
salesdocument = lv_order_id


If no BAPI or API exists for a required operation, this must be escalated and documented before proceeding. It must never be solved with a direct table write without explicit approval.

  • Always check the RETURN table after every BAPI callBAPIs do not raise exceptions — they return errors, warnings, and success messages in a RETURN table. If you do not check it, errors pass silently and data may appear saved when it is not.
CALL FUNCTION 'BAPI_SALESORDER_CHANGE'
EXPORTING salesdocument = lv_order_id
TABLES return = lt_return.​

✅Always check for errors in the return table

READ TABLE lt_return
WITH KEY type = 'E'
TRANSPORTING NO FIELDS.

IF sy-subrc = 0.
" Error found — do not commit, handle it
RAISE EXCEPTION TYPE zcx_bapi_error.
ENDIF.
  • Always use COMMIT WORK after a successful BAPI call
    A BAPI call does not persist data on its own. You must explicitly commit the work unit. Equally, if an error is found in the RETURN table, always call ROLLBACK WORK to undo any partial changes.
    "✅ Commit only after confirming no errors
CALL FUNCTION 'BAPI_TRANSACTION_COMMIT'
EXPORTING wait = abap_true.​

" ✅ Rollback on error
CALL FUNCTION 'BAPI_TRANSACTION_ROLLBACK'.
Never use COMMIT WORK directly in BAPI-based flows — always use BAPI_TRANSACTION_COMMIT with WAIT = ABAP_TRUE to ensure the update task completes before proceeding.


⚠️This rule applies to classic ABAP and BAPI-based flows only. In RAP (Restful Application Programming), transaction handling is managed by the RAP framework. Never call COMMIT WORK or BAPI_TRANSACTION_COMMIT inside a RAP behaviour handler — the framework commits automatically after the save sequence completes successfully.


17. Deployment & Transport
This here changes from company to company. Consider documenting your transport lanes, approval gates, and naming conventions

18. Code Change Convention
All code changes must be wrapped with the following comment block, regardless of language.

*** <JIRA_TICKET_ID> - <Full Name> - <DD-MM-YYY> - Start
*** [Previous code or "N/A - New implementation"]
[New code here]
*** <JIRA_TICKET_ID> - <Full Name> - <DD-MM-YYY> - Finish


19. Inline Code Comments
When to Comment explain why, not what. The code should explain what it does. Comments explain decisions.

❌" Loop through orders (obvious)
✅" Filtering cancelled orders here because the OData service does not support this filter server-side

Your turn!

Do you use AI instructions with your team? What would you add to this list? What would you change or throw out? 

Update
Well... Something happened with the instructions AI had one set of instructions and broke it fearlessly — then apologised!

entry.title: Update on SAPUI5 / OpenUI5 2.x: Best-Practice Code Is Your Best Strategy
entry.content:
In late 2023, we introduced OpenUI5 2.x with a clear goal: renew the UI5 framework by removing deprecated libraries and functionality, making it leaner, faster, and future-proof. Since then, the UI5 team has made significant progress towards this legacy-free vision — from cleaning up the core to providing tooling that helps you modernize your applications. This post is an update on where we stand with SAPUI5 / OpenUI5 2.x and what it means for you.

 

SAPUI5 / OpenUI5 2.x delivery is on hold

UI5 2.x is currently on hold from a delivery perspective. The technical work is largely done. We have cleaned up the framework, removed synchronous APIs, eliminated globals, and followed internally the same rules we ask you to follow externally. The migration tooling achieves a very high percentage of automatic conversion rates for application code. From a pure readiness standpoint, we could ship.

However, the rapid evolution of AI has fundamentally changed the questions we need to answer. What does the future programming model look like for an AI-native user experience? How should application design evolve? How do we best address the challenges and opportunities that AI brings to UI development? UI5 2.x is legacy-free, and that has clear advantages — but it is not fundamentally different from the current stack. From an AI perspective, it would not solve additional problems compared to what UI5 1.x already provides today. If we want to bring something genuinely new, addressing different problems, we likely need to do more than what version 2.x set out to do.

We have therefore decided to put the delivery on hold and use this opportunity to explore how the UI5 framework can be positioned to play a best-in-class role in an AI-driven environment.

SAPUI5 remains SAP's strategic UI technology for building applications. We want to make sure it continues to play a key role in the AI age.

The foundational work pays off

While the delivery of SAPUI5 2.x as a separate version is on hold, the foundational work we have done is far from wasted — it is already paying off today.

  • Legacy-free cleanup across the stack. We have cleaned up the UI5 core, synchronous module loading (to the extent possible in a compatible way) and globals, and deprecating non-compliant APIs. The basic UI5 libraries are legacy-free, the SAP Fiori launchpad provides a new sandbox with async services, and the SAP Fiori elements cleanup is underway.
  • UI5 linter. With a single command, you get an audit of your application that that tells you what needs to be corrected to comply with UI5 best practices. The linter also includes an autofix capability for deterministic fixes.
  • UI5 Modernization AI skills. What the linter cannot fix automatically, AI takes further. The UI5 Modernization Plugin for coding agents (e.g. for Claude Code or GitHub Copilot) run the linter, scan for solutions, and execute code changes to clean up your codebase. Together with the UI5 Linter autofix option, this achieves a very high percentage of automated migrations to legacy-free best practices. While manual testing is still required, we continue to close the remaining gaps.

These tools and the cleaned-up codebase benefit you regardless of how the UI5 versioning evolves. Following UI5 best practices — TypeScript first, asynchronous loading, no globals — makes your applications better, future-proof and ready for what comes next.

What you should do

The message is clear: keep modernizing your applications. The foundational work towards legacy-free is valuable today and will carry forward.

  1. Follow UI5 best practices: TypeScript first, asynchronous loading, no globals, no deprecated APIs.
  2. Use the UI5 linter to audit your applications against UI5 best practices.
  3. Use the UI5 Modernization Plugin with your coding agent to automate the migration to best-practice-compliant code.

Everything you do to modernize your applications today benefits you now — cleaner code, better performance, improved security, easier updates — and prepares you for the future.

Stay informed

This blog post is the official communication channel for updates on SAPUI5 / OpenUI5 2.x. When there is news to share, the UI5 team will add updates here. Subscribing to this blog post is sufficient to stay informed.

entry.title: SAP UX Update for SAP S/4HANA Cloud Private Edition 2025 FPS02
entry.content:
AI is taking user experience to the next level for SAP S/4HANA Cloud Private Edition. The first version of Joule Work brings new engagement layer experiences to users. For existing application experiences, we are introducing several AI-assisted capabilities with 2025 FPS02, such as natural language for enterprise search in the SAP Fiori launchpad and easy filtering of SAP Fiori elements based list reports . We have also infused AI further into our design and development tools for creating great UX. AI is not everything: we have also enhanced the Manage News app for My Home to provide a “required reading” feature, as well as providing a series of one-minute “Fast with SAP Fiori” videos with tips and tricks for end users.

In case you missed it, here is my previous post covering the initial 2025 release of SAP S/4HANA Cloud Private Edition:

  • SAP User Experience Update: What’s New for SAP S/4HANA 2025 (Private Cloud and On-Premise)

Here is the list of topics covered below, in order of appearance:

Joule Work
AI-Assisted UX
    -  AI-Assisted Enterprise Search
    -  AI-Assisted Easy Filter
    -  AI-Assisted Smart Summarization
    -  AI-Assisted Error Explanation
My Home
    -  Manage News App: Required Reading and Usability Improvements
Fast with SAP Fiori: One-Minute Videos for End-Users
UI Design and Technology News

 

Joule Work

Joule Work provides an AI-based user experience that transforms your way of working. With Joule work, people express what they want to accomplish, and Joule Work surfaces the right insights, automates routine work, and coordinates AI agents across systems to achieve it – all in one dynamic workspace. It acts as an engagement layer that spans across SAP products and beyond, and coexists with current experiences provided by pre-defined application UIs.

It represents a new way of interacting with business systems, since it provides:

  • One single place where a user can get tasks done, rather than the traditional app-centric interaction model, where users need to navigate to different applications or even to different products.
  • An intent-driven, situational experience, where users state their intentions in natural language and the system builds on the fly to meet their needs, taking the current business and user context (the current situation and their authorizations) into account: fetching data, triggering AI agents, and visualizing the outcome appropriately.

User-led adoption: Joule Work complements existing application UIs. This lets you and your users adopt AI at your own pace. Users decide where AI can help them. They continue to use application UIs – such as SAP Fiori apps and SAP GUI transactions accessed through the SAP Fiori launchpad - to independently verify agent actions, to extend beyond the agent’s current capabilities, or when familiar screens are simply more comfortable for familiar tasks. Embedded AI features in SAP Fiori apps help encourage users into working the AI way more frequently.

Figure 1: Joule Work experiences: Conversations, Spaces, and Develop. Alt Text: The image shows 3 screenshots, one each for the three experiences. The top of the image has a heading  “Joule Work”, above a row with five attributes: Dynamic, Proactive, Agentic, Intent-based, Omnipresent.

Joule Work provides these experiences:

  • Conversations: this experience allows people to express intent and explore what they want to accomplish through dialogue with Joule Work. It is an AI-powered chat supporting role-based intents, multiple conversation threads, with type-ahead, auto-suggestions and multi-facetted types of responses (text, tables, charts etc.). Joule Work brings together guidance and outcomes from across SAP and third-party systems. Conversations can also act as an entry point to Spaces for more complex workflows.
  • Spaces: provides flexible AI-generated spaces that dynamically adapt content based on user intent and context, for dealing with simple as well as complex tasks and issues. Each space is composed in real time to bring the right data, tools, and context together for a specific goal, allowing people to work in an environment that adapts to their present goal, instead of navigating applications and their pre-defined UIs.​
  • Develop: this experience is provided by Joule Studio, enabling developers to vibe-code, test and deploy AI agents, applications, and automations across SAP and third-party systems. Joule Work provides a convenient entry point to Joule Studio for developers and business users alike, giving them an AI-powered user experience for pro-code and low-code tools.

The Joule Work user experience is available on different kinds of clients (device types), optimized for the device’s capabilities. Three such modalities of Joule Work are available: in the web browser, on mobile devices (tablet, phone) via Joule Work mobile app, and on desktop (laptop, PC) via Joule Work desktop.

Find out more about Joule Work to get a better idea of these experiences:

  • SAP UX Update: The New Joule Work Engagement Layer Experiences
  • Joule Work on sap.com
  • Documentation: Joule Work

This blog post from my series covering public cloud UX innovations gives more information about Joule Work desktop, Joule Work mobile app, as well as SAP Build Work Zone:

  • SAP UX Q3/2026 Update – Part 1: AI, Joule, Mobile, SAP Build Work Zone

Joule Work is planned to become available later this month (October) to SAP S/4HANA Cloud Private Edition 2023 FPS03 and upward, as well as 2025 FPS01 and upward, with SAP-managed Joule and SAP-managed integration of Joule to the SAP S/4HANA Cloud Private Edition.

 

AI-Assisted UX

The following embedded AI features are now all generally available with SAP S/4HANA Cloud Private Edition 2025 FPS02, and included in Base, and hence included in your regular license. There’s no additional cost, and no AI Unit usage involved.

AI-Assisted Enterprise Search

You can now use natural language in the search field available at the top of every screen in SAP S/4HANA Cloud Private Edition, making it even easier to benefit from powerful enterprise search capabilities. With enterprise search, you can find the business objects such as sales orders, deliveries, and invoices directly – as you can see in Figure 2.

Important design principles for us for AI is “human in the loop” and “explainability”. In this case, we display the filters at the top of the search list that AI has identified from the query, so that users can confirm that AI has indeed understood the intent correctly.

Figure 2: AI-assisted enterprise search, showing how you can easily find business data directly using natural language. Alt Text: A short video showing how a user can enter in the search field in the shell header bar “Show me sales orders over 325k usd” and get a corresponding list sales orders. The user than adds the text “open” resulting in a list with fewer results.

Watch the full video:

  • Video:  AI-Assisted Enterprise Search in SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition  (0:45 min.)

AI-Assisted Easy Filter

This is another example of interacting via natural language with your application:  in SAP S/4HANA Cloud Private Edition, you can now easily filter lists using natural language, rather than manually setting the filters for each field in the filter bar. We use SAP Business AI to interpret the query and identify the appropriate filter values. As with AI-assisted enterprise search, we keep the human in the loop and provide explainability: the filter values identified are displayed at the top of the list, so users can get confirmation that their text has been correctly interpreted. Figure 6 shows an example.

Figure 3: AI-assisted easy filter allows you to filter business data using natural language. ALT Text: The Manage Sales Orders – Version 2 app is shown with one text entry field above the list of orders, containing the text “In process orders for customer cbont for delivery this month”. To the right of the text field the “Go” button has the AI icon on the left of the Go text. Below the text entry field identified filters are shown: Overall Status “In Process”, Requested Delivery Date “01.10.2026…31.10.2026, Sold-to Party: CBont Industries”.

From a technical perspective, it is available for SAP Fiori elements list reports – with names along the lines of “Manage <insert your business object here>” apps (for example: Manage Sales Orders)

In addition to filtering, you can use natural language for sorting and grouping.

Sorting and grouping means that you can use natural language to say how you want the result to be sorted, and you can also specify how you want the entries in the table to be grouped.

Figure 4 shows an example with the Manage Sales Orders – Version 2 app, where the user has typed in “Show me sales orders in status open or in process where the net value is >= 50K EUR sorted by net value ascending and grouped by overall status”. Below the line containing the prompt you can see how the app shows the filters that have been identified from the text: overall status (2 values), net value >= 50000, document currency European Euro. The data in the table is sorted and grouped as requested, the first group showing the open orders, the second group those that are in process.

Figure 4: Sorting and grouping with AI-Assisted Easy Filter. Alt-Text: Screenshot showing a list of sales orders with natural language filter request and outcome as described in the above text.

View management: You can save your natural language based filter as a view for the application, just as you have always been able to save views for filters based on defined individual field values in the filter bar.

Watch it in action here, including examples of grouping and view management::

  • Video: AI-Assisted Easy Filter (1:30 min.)

AI-Assisted Easy Filter is available for applications based on SAP Fiori elements, Web Dynpro for ABAP, and Floorplan Manager applications.

AI-Assisted Smart Summarization

Users of SAP S/4HANA Cloud Private Edition can use the new smart summarization capability to generate personalizable summaries of object pages based on SAP Fiori elements. You simply select the sections you want to have included in the summary, and let smart summarization create a summary for you. You can edit the result and copy it into your clipboard with just one click, ready to paste into an e-mail, chat or document. Figure 5 shows an example of a summary. If you want to see how to select the sections, watch this:

  • Video: AI-Assisted Smart Summarization (1:00 min.)

Figure 5: AI-Assisted Smart Summarization generates summaries of object pages based on SAP Fiori elements in SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition 2502. ALT Text: A popover is shown with formatted text, the Header saying “Standard Order Summary of 212298”, followed by a brief description and then sections for “Data, Location and Address”, with five bullet points for requested delivery date, document, pricing, and billing dates, and shipping address, “Key Highlights”, showing overall status, overall block status, incompletion status and more.

AI-Assisted Error Explanation

New users who are unfamiliar with the system may find that the short error messages give too little information for them to fully understand the issue, and what to do about it. This is where the AI-Assisted Error Explanation in SAP S/4HANA Cloud Private Edition can help: it uses SAP Business AI to summarize information which explains the error and provide a recommendation for how to resolve it. Figure 6 shows an example where a user has entered a Sold-to-Party ID which does not exist in the system.

This feature is available for applications based on SAP Fiori elements.

Figure 6: AI-Assisted Error Explanation. ALT Text: On the left the field “Sold-to Party containing “ABC” is marked red, below that a  popover with an error message “No customer master record exists for sold-to-party AABC”, and in the text line below that the AI icon followed by “Explain link. An arrow leads from this link to a popover, which indicates what happens when you click on this text: you get a popover with an short “Understanding the issue” section and a longer “Resolving the issue” section with a list of actions.

Have a look:

  • Video: AI-Assisted Error Explanation (40 seconds)

List of Supported AI-Assisted SAP Fiori Apps

This SAP note has an Excel file attached that lists all the SAP Fiori apps that support Easy Filter, Smart Summarization, and Easy Fill:

  • SAP Note: 3692870 - Configuration of Base AI-Assisted Features in SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition.

Although the note refers to the Public Edition, it does also apply to those Fiori apps listed there that are available in the Private Edition.

Find out more:

To get started with these AI-assisted features, have a look at this great blog post from Jocelyn Dart, as well as the documentation:

  • SAP Fiori for SAP S/4HANA – Getting started with Base AI-assisted Features in 2025 FPS2
  • There’s help for your administrator in the SAP Fiori launchpad > Administration guide section Enabling AI-assisted features.
  • And help for your users in the SAP Fiori launchpad > User guide section Using AI-Assisted Features.

Of course, you will want to tell your users all about these new AI-assisted features and encourage them to try them out! A great way to pass on the latest news and tips is via the Manage News app – where you post news for users to see in their Display News tile in their My Home page.

If you haven’t configured this yet, as usual your administrator will find the instructions in the SAP Fiori launchpad > Administration guide section Manage News.

 

Manage News App now with “Must be Read” Feature

News articles containing essential company information can now be designated as required reading. All users must acknowledge that they have read and understood the content.

The main benefits of this feature are:

  • Strengthens accountability: When reading is mandatory, employees can be held accountable for understanding essential information. This practice helps ensure compliance with legal, safety, and policy-related requirements.
  • Ensures consistent knowledge across the organization: All employees receive the same information, minimizing knowledge gaps and miscommunication.
  • Enhances change management : During periods of transition—such as the introduction of new policies or process changes—required reading ensures that all employees understand the reasons behind and the impacts of those changes.

Figure 7 shows what this looks like for a user: a required reading pop-over appears on their screen. The article has also been flagged as “Containing Critical News”.

Figure 7: An example of a news article that is required reading. Alt Text: A screenshot of My Home with a pop-over “Required Reading” that is also highlighted with “Contains Critical News”. The news article has an image at the top, followed by text showing the first part of the article. The “Done” button is greyed out, the “Remind me later” button is visible.

Figure 8 below shows the Manage News app, with the toggles Critical and the new Required Reading one.

Figure 8: The Manage News app has a toggle to mark articles as “Required Reading”. Alt Text: Screenshot of the Manage News app with the toggles set to “Yes”, and some news text in the Description field.

Get an overview of the Manage News app, including the required reading feature:

  • Video: Manage News Application in My Home (1:55 min.)
  • Video: Manage News: Required Reading (1:00 min.)

Fast with SAP Fiori: one-minute videos for end-users

SAP Fiori apps help users work quickly and efficiently – especially when they take advantage of the many time-saving features that are built in. We have found that users are often not aware of some of these features, so to mitigate that, we now provide several one-minute videos for users.

You can have a look at them using this link, which takes you to the landing page displayed in Figure 9:

  • Fast with SAP Fiori – One tip, one minute.

Since we want to help the actual users of the system, we have made them directly accessible via the built-in help within SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition, as shown in Figure 9 further below.

Figure 9: Fast with SAP Fiori landing page. Alt Text: a screenshot of the web page with two rows of cards: first a card for Additional Languages, followed by ten cards, one for each video, with a thumbnail screenshot, title and brief description.

At the time of writing we provide the ten videos featured in Figure 8, covering the following topics:

  1. Perform Actions on Table Items
    How to use the context menu in a table to trigger relevant actions.
  2. Copy and Paste in Tables
    How to copy whole lines, sections or cells of a table, and how to paste data into tables.
  3. Manage Favorites in My Home
    How to manage your favorite apps in the My Home page: adding apps, grouping them, changing the color as well as removing apps.
  4. Find Keyboard Shortcuts
    How to display the keyboard shortcuts available to you on the section of the screen you are currently using.
  5. Personalize the Table Layout
    How to define and store specific table layouts: hide, add, reorder columns, sort, filter and group entries, and save the layout for reuse.
  6. Adapt the UI (for key users)
    How to adapt the layout of the UI, and also how to change the text arrangement in fields that contain both ID and description: you can choose to show “ID (description)”, “description (ID)”, or only “ID” or only “description”.
  7. Finding Apps
    How to find applications – recent activities, frequently used, or using search.
  8. Saving Filter Values as Views
    How to save specific filter values as reusable views, and how to share them with colleagues if needed.
  9. Adapt your User Settings
    How to change settings such as appearance (light / dark), date format, time zone, decimal format, and how you can personalize search.
  10. Set Default Values
    How to define default values for IDs such as your company code, sales organization etc., so that you don’t have to enter them every time in filters etc.

The videos are in English, but we offer dubbed versions in these languages:

  • Chinese
  • French
  • German
  • Italian
  • Japanese
  • Portugese
  • Spanish

For those of you who prefer using YouTube, we now have a playlist for all these videos:

  • YouTube Video Playlist: Fast with SAP Fiori: One Tip Per Minute

If you would like to see some additional tips and tricks for users that are not yet covered by the above series, have a look at the video contained in my blog post from 2023. I have listed the timings of these additional tips below:

  • SAP Fiori: Tips & Tricks for Users of SAP S/4HANA
    • 00:00 SAP Fiori launchpad, editing your pages (personalizing) – this is for the pages in launchpad spaces, not for the My Home page, which is covered by Fast with SAP Fiori.

    • 20:20 Working with applications Quick Tour.

The blog post lists the timings of all the tips at the end, many of which are covered by Fast with SAP Fiori.

This last year we have continued investing in our UI design and technology, adding AI capabilities to make it even easier to create new application experiences, as well as providing new features. Some of the highlights are:
